rows.explanation: The required read/write channels, server-derived auth, scoped authorization, and private row mapping are coherent. However, labels are scattered across architecture-wide roots, and simple CRUD gains a repository port plus one forwarding use-case wrapper per operation.

The proposal keeps CRUD direct and uses the correct RSC, GET, and Server Action channels with server-side authentication and RLS. Capability code is dispersed across app/actions, app/components, and a generic lib bucket; combining server persistence internals and product types in lib/labels.ts only partially establishes a browser-safe boundary.

The runtime channels, direct local-store access, authorization, and private mapping are strong. Capability behavior is fragmented across domain, data, adapters, client-cache, and UI roots, while the shared define-boundary abstraction acts as a universal validation/failure/result wrapper.

This proposal colocates capability behavior under src/modules/labels while leaving route glue in app, avoids speculative layers, uses direct server-only RSC reads, a cacheable GET for browser reads, and top-level Server Actions for writes. It also clearly separates browser-safe code from private mapped store rows and enforces server-derived identity, policy checks, scoped caching, and RLS.

Cohesive labels slice with route-private glue in app, no speculative port or per-operation layer, correct direct RSC/GET/Server Action channels, server-derived authentication with RLS authorization, and private row mapping.

The runtime flows, security boundaries, direct repository CRUD, and private mapping are coherent. Colocation is only partial because behavior is split between app/labels and a generic lib bucket, which also triggers the shared/lib penalty.

Uses the required runtime channels, strong server-side auth, and private mapping, but scatters one small capability across architectural roots. The boundary declaration is a universal wrapper, and the entries layer adds some unnecessary application indirection despite avoiding separate operation files and a repository port.

Security and mapping are strong, but the small CRUD feature is widely scattered and adds a speculative repository port plus one use-case wrapper per operation. The proposed labels.route.ts is outside app and is not a valid App Router route.ts location, so the required browser GET cannot be registered as designed.

The policy and provider seam are framework-neutral, and the SSE lifecycle correctly covers cancellation, idle timeout, commit-aware failures, and safe provider mapping. Placement is scattered across generic top-level layers rather than one capability root. It also explicitly applies the same generic boundary wrapper to HTTP streaming and jobs, weakening their native contracts.

The proposal coherently colocates assistant behavior, defines a framework-neutral operation and capability port, and gives SSE and jobs distinct native adapters. It correctly handles abort propagation, per-read idle timeout, post-commit failure events, report-once behavior, redaction, and retry/dead-letter decisions without provider leakage or a universal wrapper.

The runtime flow satisfies the essential SSE, cancellation, idle-timeout, failure, and job requirements, and keeps provider details private. However, assistant behavior is spread across generic application, domain, and infrastructure roots. The stated generic result/event abstraction is shared across HTTP streaming and jobs and even carries commit state, constituting the prohibited universal wrapper despite transport-specific mapping.

The design uses a cohesive assistant capability root with justified Route Handler and worker surfaces. It preserves a framework-neutral generation operation and provider-neutral port, handles abort and idle timeout correctly, changes failure representation after commitment, reports unexpected failures once, and retains separate HTTP, SSE, and job contracts while sharing only semantic primitives.

The Route Handler, abort propagation, idle watchdog, commit-aware SSE failure, job semantics, and provider isolation are coherent. However, assistant behavior is scattered across application, domain, infrastructure, and jobs rather than colocated under one capability root.

The application operation, provider port, native channel contracts, and safe failure taxonomy are strong. However, the claimed Route Handler is placed under src/adapters rather than app or src/app, so Next.js will not expose it; consequently the proposed concrete tree cannot provide the required browser stream without an omitted framework route.

The proposal clearly provides a valid SSE Route Handler, framework-neutral use case, abort-aware provider port, gap-based idle timeout, commit-aware errors, report-once ownership, and native job outcomes. Its files are organized by global layers rather than one capability root.

The proposal colocates behavior under src/modules/assistant with a justified App Router entrypoint, keeps generation framework-neutral behind a capability-shaped port, handles the full SSE lifecycle correctly, preserves native stream and job contracts, and confines provider details to a private adapter.

Board-specific policy is coherently centralized in a route-private loader, and capability independence and authorization are preserved. However, it explicitly avoids a board capability, lacks board-language ports, exposes only a route-private rather than public board surface, and does not clearly specify once-only reporting for unexpected failures. Its claimed parallel label loading also conflicts with constraining the query to label IDs obtained from work-items, but this is correctable and not fatal.

A dedicated board use-case owns orchestration and policy, depends on board-local reader ports, and is wired to narrow trusted capability surfaces. The RSC route calls a board-specific server entrypoint, both capabilities retain authorization and persistence ownership, board policy fails closed, and infrastructure failures are recorded and safely mapped at one boundary.

The board slice clearly owns policy and orchestration, the dependency graph is acyclic, the RSC route uses a board-specific entrypoint, and failure reporting is explicitly centralized once while authorization remains layered. The ports criterion is only partial because the design expressly rejects board-owned ports and directly calls published capability operations, although those operations are narrow public surfaces rather than internals.

Route-local board logic preserves capability independence, uses trusted APIs, and applies board security policy. It is only a partial match because it avoids a board capability and board-owned ports, equivocates between orchestration directly in the page and an optional private helper, and describes diagnostics without clearly establishing once-only reporting. Its fail-closed omission of affected items prevents disclosure, so the design is not fatally insecure.

The page, not a board capability, owns the cross-capability policy and directly composes the two APIs. The capability APIs are narrow and preserve an acyclic graph with private stores, but dependencies are not expressed through a board-owned boundary. Authorization is coherent, while unexpected-failure reporting is not explicitly once-only.

A board slice clearly owns policy and orchestration, the route uses a single board read boundary, both capabilities stay independent, and authorization plus once-only reporting are explicit. It deliberately omits board-owned ports and consumes capability operation surfaces directly, so the board-language dependency criterion is only partial.

The proposal gives the board a focused use case, board-language ports, and outbound adapters over independent public capability contracts. The RSC route uses a board DAL entrypoint, authorization is enforced at all relevant ownership boundaries, inaccessible label data is rejected from the DTO, and unexpected failures are reported once.

Route-private board code clearly owns the policy and exposes one loader to the RSC page. Work-items and labels remain acyclic behind narrow trusted server surfaces, with layered authorization and once-only unexpected-failure reporting. The design lacks board-language ports or adapters, making that rubric item partial.
